newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: ALPINE SKIING-REITER EMERGES FROM SLOW LANE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-REITER EMERGES FROM SLOW LANE.

text.p: At a time when ski racers his age were celebrating World Cup victories, Mario Reiter was still paying for his training by feeding cows.
Now, five years later, after winning two World Cup races and a silver medal at the world championships in Sierra Nevada, the 26-year-old is one of Austria's biggest hopes of the winter.

Despite failing to impress at the season's opening giant slalom in Soelden last month, where he finished 27th after losing a contact lense in the second run, Reiter was among the fastest in Austrian training sessions this northern summer.
The man, who joined his country's elite team at the late age of 21, now enjoys the privilege of a guaranteed starting place in each of the season's slalom and giant slalom races.
Llife was not always so sweet for an introvert from the town of Rankweil in Austria's western province of Vorarlberg.
At 19 he was dropped from all Austrian ski squads after tearing his left cruciate ligament twice.
Reiter fought back, training alone on the Kaunertal glacier in Austria and taking a part-time job at a nearby farm while continuing with his formal education.
"I was on my own during this time and I learned how to look after myself. I suppose that's why now I am considered the black sheep of the team who sticks to himself," Reiter said in an interview.
"But I see this positively. In ski racing, you train and travel to events as a team, but up there in the starthouse and on the slope you are completely on your own."
Two years after re-joining his national squad and failing to secure a regular place on the World Cup team, Reiter enlisted Valentin Hobel to aid him with his mental preparation.

Since then, consistent good results have established him on the circuit. His maiden World Cup victory at a giant slalom in Furano, Japan, in the 1994-95 season earned him the nickname "Super Mario" in the Austrian media.
Last winter, he won the night slalom at Sestriere, Italy, and finished eighth in the overall standings, as well as clinching slalom silver at the world championships in Spain.

"I realised I would have to do more than just physical training. People laughed at me at first -- they called him (Hobel) my psychologist -- but now they are stunned when they see my results," he said.
"To win ski races you need good equipment, you have to be fit and have a good environment in your team. But, what is most important, is you need to be strong mentally."
What impresses Hobel most about Reiter is "the stark contrast between his modesty in life and his iron determination of wanting to achieve everything".
"Mario can control his aggression and use it at the right moments. He also has an incredible drive in him. These are his strengths," said Hobel, who now accompanies Reiter to most World Cup races.
On the slopes, Reiter punches his way through the gates. Off-piste he is quiet and soft-spoken.
"Aggression is good for sport but bad in your private life," Reiter said. "It should be kept locked away and called up only during competition."
Reiter's goals are medals at the 1997 Sestriere world championships and at the 1998 Nagano Olympics in the combination, giant slalom or his favorite discipline, the slalom.

"It would be utopic of me to want to set records at my age -- like winning more slaloms than other skier," he said. "But I would give my championship medal for a victory in the Kitzbuehel slalom. It is the oldest and most traditional race with the most flair."

At some stage, Reiter would also like to aim for the overall World Cup title. "If I have a lot of points towards the end of the season then I'll try my luck in super-G. If not, then the overalls will have to wait."
Winning is not everything for the Austrian.

"I want to give people a positive image of ski racing. What is important is what you make of a job. If I can leave something positive behind -- like become an idol for children -- then I know I did my job correctly."

Reiter also feels ski racers should do more to entertain spectators at events. Consequently his professionally organized "Super Mario" fan club, dance and chant Austrian folk songs on race days in Soelden wearing colourful, self-tailored national costumes.
"People stand in the cold all day to support us. It is our duty to make them feel they are an important aspect, which they are, races without spectators are boring.
"The sport gives us skiers so much we should give something back in return. The ski circus needs more characters like (Alberto) Tomba.
"I'm not saying the majority of skiers are boring but many just don't bother. I admire all winners but winning alone is not enough," he said.

When he retires from ski racing in three to four years time, Reiter plans to become a primary school teacher. "Skiing is an important part of my life but it is not everything. There are other more important things like family and kids."

In his spare time, Reiter enjoys climbing, listening to music and reading literature. "I read a lot in order to maintain a certain intellectual level, which unfortunately can easily be lost in the ski racing world," he said.
